rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The damned are not put to death and do not die, so their punishment continues without relief.
rows.anchor: لا يقضى عليهم ميتين، إنما يقضى عليهم ولا يموتون

rows.speaker: عيسى، والحسن
rows.claim: They read «فيموتون» with nūn, coordinating it with «لا يقضى»; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this reading weak.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عيسى، والحسن: فيموتون، بالنون

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان المازني
rows.claim: He takes the coordination to mean they do not die, paralleling the denied permission to apologize; their punishment is not eased.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عثمان المازني: هو عطف، أي فلا يموتون

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: ʿAbd al-Wārith’s reading from Abū ʿAmr leaves the fāʾ of «يخفف» unvowelled, treating a separated form like a connected one; he cites poetry.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الوارث عن أبي عمرو: ولا يخفف بإسكان الفاء

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «نَجزي كل» actively, with «كل» accusative; Abū ʿAmr and Abū Ḥātim from Nāfiʿ read it passively, with «كل» nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: نجزي كل، مبنيا للفاعل، ونصب كل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb «يصطرخون» is an intensive form from ṣarakh, with tāʾ changed to ṭāʾ; ṣarākh is a loud cry, also used for appealing for help.
rows.anchor: وهم يصطرخون: بني من الصرخ يفتعل، وأبدلت من التاء طاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their plea asks to leave Hell and return to worldly life.
rows.anchor: ربنا أخرجنا: أي قائلين ربنا أخرجنا منها، أي من النار، وردنا إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He explains the promised righteous deed as professing «لا إله إلا الله», abandoning shirk, believing instead of disbelieving, and obeying instead of sinning.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: نقل: لا إله إلا الله، غير الذي كنا نعمل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He asks why the request adds «other than what we used to do» after «righteous deeds», and whether it implies a different righteous deed; Abū Ḥayyān says it conveys regret and admission.
rows.anchor: وما فائدة زيادة غير الذي كنا نعمل على أنه يوهم أنهم يعملون صالحا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added phrase intensifies regret for their former wrong; its apparent implication disappears because they had treated shirk and sins as good and now seek different conduct.
rows.anchor: فائدته زيادة التحسر على ما عملوه من غير الصالح مع الاعتراف به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says they receive this answer after a period equal to worldly life; «أولم نعمركم» is a rebuke, confirmation, and reminder.
rows.anchor: روي أنهم يجابون بعد مقدار الدنيا: أولم نعمركم، وهو استفهام توبيخ وتوقيف وتقرير

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «ما يتذكر»; al-Aʿmash reads «ما يذكر» by assimilation from «اذكر», pronouncing the initial hamzat al-waṣl in connected recitation.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ما يتذكر فيه من تذكر. وقرأ الأعمش: ما يذكر فيه

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He identifies the lifetime sufficient for reflection as the age of maturity, the beginning of discernment.
rows.anchor: البلوغ، يريد أنه أول حال التذكر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He gives eighteen years as the lifetime sufficient for reflection.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ثمان عشرة سنة

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
rows.claim: He gives twenty years as the lifetime sufficient for reflection.
rows.anchor: وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز: عشرون

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He gives forty years; other reported ages are seventeen, fifty, and sixty, the last attributed to ʿAlī and also transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أربعون وقيل: خمسون. وقال علي: ستون، وروي ذلك عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «And a warner came to you» coordinates with «Did We not give you life?», whose implied meaning is affirmative, as in the cited Qurʾānic examples.
rows.anchor: وجاءكم معطوف على أولم نعمركم، لأن معناه: قد عمرناكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «The warner» is generic for the prophets, each warning his own community; another recitation has the plural «النذر».
rows.anchor: والنذير جنس، وهم الأنبياء، كل نبي نذير أمته. وقرىء: النذر جمعا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، وعكرمة، وسفيان، ووكيع، والحسن بن الفضل، والفراء، والطبري
rows.claim: They explain the warner as gray hair; other explanations are deaths among relatives and reaching extreme old age.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النذير: الشيب، قاله ابن عباس، وعكرمة، وسفيان، ووكيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Taste» refers to Hell’s punishment.
rows.anchor: فذوقوا: أي عذاب جهنم

rows.speaker: جناح بن حبيش
rows.claim: He reads «عالم غيب» with tanwīn and accusative «غيب»; the majority use the genitive construction.
rows.anchor: وقرأ جناح بن حبيش: عالم منونا، غيب نصبا والجمهور: على الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s knowledge of the unseen explains the preceding judgment: He knows hidden thoughts and knew the disbelievers’ rejection was so entrenched they would never believe.
rows.anchor: فلا يخفى عليه ما تنطوى عليه المصدور من المضمرات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Successors» can be plural of khalīfa or khalīf; humanity replaces earlier peoples, yet fails to learn from destroyed deniers of the messengers.
rows.anchor: وخلائف: جمع خليفة، وخلفاء: جمع خليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A disbeliever bears the punishment of his disbelief; the address is apparently general, though some restrict it to Meccans.
rows.anchor: فعليه كفره: أي عقاب كفره، والظاهر أنه خطاب عام وقيل: لأهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Maqt» means the strongest contempt, hatred, and anger; loss is loss of a lifetime spent outside obedience, exchanged for God’s wrath and Hell instead of reward.
rows.anchor: والمقت: أشد الاحتقار والبغض والغضب، والخسار: خسار العمر

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: The interrogative alif in «Have you seen your partners?» serves to elicit confirmation.
rows.anchor: قال الحوفي: ألف الاستفهام ذلك للتقرير

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Following Sībawayh, he treats «Have you seen?» as equivalent to «tell me».
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: أرأيتم ينزل عند سيبويه منزلة أخبروني

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He parses «Show me» as a substitute for «Have you seen?»: tell what the partners created independently, whether they share in creating the heavens, or possess a scripture authorizing partnership and intercession.
rows.anchor: أروني بدل من أرأيتم لأن معنى أرأيتم أخبروني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects al-Zamakhsharī’s substitution analysis: an interrogative particle should recur with a substitute, sentence-for-sentence substitution is unattested, and the required repeated governor is absent.
rows.anchor: أما قوله: أروني بدل من أرأيتم فلا يصح، لأنه إذا أبدل مما دخل عليه الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He takes «Have you seen?» as «tell me», governing «your partners» as its first object and the embedded question «what did they create?» as the second; «show me» reinforces parenthetically.
rows.anchor: والذي أذهب إليه أن أرأيتم بمعنى أخبرني، وهي تطلب مفعولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible analysis is competing government of «what did they create?» by both verbs, with the second verb operative as Basran grammarians prefer.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون ذلك أيضا من باب الأعمال، لأنه توارد على ماذا خلقوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, «Have you seen?» may be a real question and «show me» a challenge to demonstrate the idols’ supposed power, exposing the irrationality of worshipping the powerless.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يحتمل أن يكون أرأيتم استفهاما حقيقيا، وأروني أمر تعجيز للتبيين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenged power might allegedly reside in earthly idols or heavenly beings said to help create the heavens, or in intercession; the latter would require divine authorization.
rows.anchor: أم قدرتها في الشفاعة لكم؟ كما قال بعضهم: إن الملائكة ما خلقوا شيئا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols are called «your partners» only because their worshippers made them partners; a possible alternative is partners in Hell, linked to the cited verse.
rows.anchor: وأضاف الشركاء إليهم من حيث هم جعلوهم شركاء لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in «Did We give them?» apparently refers to the alleged partners: do they have divine scripture granting intercession? Only God’s permission allows intercession.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في آتيناهم عائد على الشركاء، لتناسب الضمائر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the pronoun refers to the polytheists, shifting from direct address to distance them; neither reason nor revelation licenses worship of beings unable to create or share in creation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عائد على المشركين، ويكون التفاتا خرج من ضمير الخطاب إلى ضمير الغيبة

rows.speaker: ابن وثاب، والأعمش، وحمزة، وأبو عمرو، وابن كثير، وحفص، وأبان عن عاصم
rows.claim: They read «على بيّنة» in the singular; the rest of the seven read it in the plural.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن وثاب، والأعمش، وحمزة، وأبو عمرو، وابن كثير، وحفص، وأبان عن عاصم: على بينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse turns from the idols’ impotence to God’s majesty and power, making their insignificance clearer by contrast.
rows.anchor: ولما بين تعالى فساد أمر الأصنام ووقف الحجة على بطلانها، عقبه بذكر عظمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God holds the heavens and earth from leaving their places and the heavens from falling; he rejects the implication that the earth does not rotate.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن معناه أن تنتقلا عن أماكنها وتسقط السموات عن علوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects the alternative interpretation that God prevents the earth from rotating, noting that this would imply the earth does not rotate.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح أن الأرض لا تدور

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: His reported view is that the heavens do not rotate but the stars travel within them; rotation itself would constitute a departure.
rows.anchor: ويظهر من قول ابن مسعود: أن السماء لا تدور، وإنما تجري فيها الكواكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Lest they depart» can be purposive, with an implied «so that» or «for fear that»; al-Zajjāj instead treats it as a second object after «prevents», or as an inclusive apposition.
rows.anchor: وأن تزولا في موضع المفعول له، وقدر لئلا تزولا، وكراهة أن تزولا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional «if they departed» concerns the possible cosmic collapse at the Resurrection, or is hypothetical like «if»; Ibn Abī ʿAbla reads «even if they departed» with a negative particle.
rows.anchor: فإن قدرنا دخولها على الممكن، فيكون ذلك باعتبار يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath response «He holds them» has present force under the conditional; the conditional answer is omitted because the oath answer indicates it.
rows.anchor: وإنما هو في معنى المضارع لدخول إن الشرطية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says «He holds them» answers the oath in «if they departed» and stands in for both answers; Abū Ḥayyān objects that one expression cannot both have and lack the required grammatical position.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: وإن أمسكهما جواب القسم في ولئن زالتا، سد مسد الجوابين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first «min» in «any one» reinforces totality; «after Him» marks the starting point after God ceases to hold them.
rows.anchor: ومن في من أحد لتأكيد الاستغراق، ومن في من بعده لابتداء الغاية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Asked what Kaʿb al-Aḥbār said, a man from Syria reported that the heavens rest on an angel’s shoulder; Ibn ʿAbbās called Kaʿb a liar and recited the verse.
rows.anchor: إن السموات على منكب ملك، قال: كذب كعب، أما ترك يهوديته بعد

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: He criticized Kaʿb al-Aḥbār’s account, saying Judaism remained lodged in his heart though nearly departing.
rows.anchor: كادت أن تفارقه

rows.speaker: طائفة
rows.claim: One group says God is described as forbearing and forgiving because the heavens and earth nearly split from shirk; He restrains them by judgment while allowing believers time to repent.
rows.anchor: اتصافه بالحلم والغفران في هذه الآية إنما هو إشارة إلى أن السماء كادت تزول

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains the forbearance and forgiveness as God’s delaying punishment while holding the heavens together, though they deserve to be shaken by the word of shirk.
rows.anchor: حليما غفورا، غير معاجل بالعقوبة، حيث يمسكها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ones who swore were Quraysh; after their rejection of monotheism, the passage describes their denial of messengers.
rows.anchor: الضمير في وأقسموا لقريش. ولما بين إنكارهم للتوحيد، بين تكذيبهم للرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They used to condemn Jews and Christians for rejecting their messengers, promising to be more guided if a warner came; when Muḥammad came, they rejected him.
rows.anchor: قيل: وكانوا يلعنون اليهود والنصارى حيث كذبوا رسلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «If a warner came to them» paraphrases their meaning, not their wording; direct quotation would say «came to us». «One of the nations» means a notably guided or peerless nation.
rows.anchor: لئن جاءهم: حكاية لمعنى كلامهم لا للفظهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warner’s arrival or his message figuratively increased their flight from truth, because it caused them to increase their own rejection.
rows.anchor: وإسناد الزيادة إليه مجاز، لأنه هو السبب في أن زادوا أنفسهم نفورا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «When» is a conjunction, not a temporal adverb: «they only increased» answers it, and a negative answer could not precede its temporal governor.
rows.anchor: وجواب لما: ما زادهم، وفيه دليل واضح على حرفية لما لا ظرفيتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «In arrogance» and «evil plotting» are causal accusatives: arrogance and scheming against the Messenger drove them from truth; the latter means deception and hostile plotting.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن استكبارا مفعول من أجله، أي سبب النفور

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He interprets «evil plotting» as shirk.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: المكر السيء هو الشرك

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: He construes «arrogance» as a substitute for «flight»; another analysis treats the words as circumstantial descriptions of their arrogance and plotting.
rows.anchor: وقيل: استكبارا بدل من نفورا، وقاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive in «evil plotting» links the adjective to its described noun, explaining the otherwise unexpected original form «evil» in the following phrase.
rows.anchor: ومكر السيء من إضافة الموصوف إلى صفته، ولذلك جاء على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible syntax coordinates «evil plotting» with «flight». Most readers pronounce the hamza vowelled; al-Aʿmash and Ḥamza leave it unvowelled.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يجوز أن يكون ومكر السيئ معطوفا على نفورا. وقرأ الجمهور

rows.speaker: الزجاج، ومحمد بن يزيد
rows.claim: They call the unvowelled reading erroneous or impossible because it drops inflectional marking; Abū Ḥayyān reports grammarians who suspected it was merely a pause in transmission.
rows.anchor: وزعم الزجاج أن هذه القراءة لحن

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: He defends the unvowelled reading by citing phonetic easing of successive vowels, poetic licence, or pronunciation as if pausing; therefore it should not simply be called erroneous.
rows.anchor: من التأويل، لم يسغ أن يقال لحن

rows.speaker: ابن القشيري
rows.claim: He says a reading established by widespread transmission or tawātur must be permissible and cannot be called erroneous.
rows.anchor: ما ثبت بالاستفاضة أو التواتر أنه قرىء به فلا بد من جوازه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He suggests the hamza may have been very briefly pronounced or followed by a slight pause before beginning the next phrase.
rows.anchor: لعله اختلس فظن سكونا، أو وقف وقفة خفيفة

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: His reported reading moves the hamza and yields «مكر السي», described as a metathesis of the softened form, with a poetic witness.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن كثير: ومكر السيء، بهمزة ساكنة بعد السين وياء بعدها مكسورة

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: He reads «and an evil plot», coordinating one indefinite with another.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن مسعود: ومكرا سيئا، عطف نكرة على نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Yahiq» means to surround and befall, and is used only for something disliked; the passive-like variant is also reported.
rows.anchor: ولا يحيق: أي يحيط ويحل، ولا يستعمل إلا في المكروه

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: Asked why plotters sometimes gain by their schemes, he gives three answers: the verse may target Quraysh’s plot against the Prophet ending at Badr; it may be general; or apparent short-term defeat is reversed by ultimate outcomes.
rows.anchor: فالجواب من وجوه: أحدها: أن المكر في الآية هو المكر بالرسول

rows.speaker: أبو عبد الله الرازي
rows.claim: He calls the general reading the soundest and cites a prophetic warning not to scheme or aid a schemer, since evil plotting ultimately returns upon its author.
rows.anchor: وثانيها: أنه عام، وهو الأصح

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: He tells Ibn ʿAbbās the proverb that one who digs a pit for his brother falls into it; Ibn ʿAbbās says this is already in the verse, paralleling an Arab proverb.
rows.anchor: إنا وجدنا هذا في كتاب الله، ولا يحيق المكر السيئ إلا بأهله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The precedent is God’s destruction of peoples who disbelieved their messengers; its wording is first attributed to those who undergo it, then to God who instituted it, and cannot be changed or diverted.
rows.anchor: وبين تعالى الانتقام من مكذبي الرسل عادة لا يبدلها بغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Meccans could see evidence of earlier peoples’ destruction on trade journeys through Syria, Iraq, and Yemen, including Thamūd’s dwellings.
rows.anchor: في مسايرهم ومتاجرهم، في رحلتهم إلى الشام والعراق واليمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the parallel passage «they were stronger» is a new assertion; here «and they were» is circumstantial, so the two passages make different points.
rows.anchor: وهناك كانوا أشد منهم قوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nothing in heaven or earth can escape or outrun God; His knowledge encompasses everything and His power makes nothing impossible.
rows.anchor: وما كان الله ليعجزه: أي ليفوته ويسبقه، من شيء: أي شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s forbearance is shown by delaying punishment for shirk and denial of messengers, as in the parallel verse from al-Naḥl.
rows.anchor: ثم ذكر تعالى حلمه تعالى على عباده في تعجيل العقوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in «its back» refers to earth: the context implies it in al-Naḥl, while this passage also names earth in the preceding phrase; its surface is likened to an animal bearing loads.
rows.anchor: والضمير عائد على الأرض، إلا أن هناك يدل عليه سياق الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God «seeing His servants» threatens the deniers with requital for their deeds.
rows.anchor: فإنه كان بعباده بصيرا: توعد للمكذبين، أي فيجازيهم بأعمالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for the camel’s raised head is glossed as lifting it after drinking water; the source promises a fuller discussion later.
rows.anchor: قمح البعير رأسه: رفعه أثر شرب الماء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: The date-stalk «ʿurjūn» is the stem from the cluster’s branches to its origin; al-Zajjāj derives the word from bending.
rows.anchor: العرجون: عود العذق من بين الشمراخ إلى منبته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Jadath» means grave; «jadf» is a variant replacing thāʾ with fāʾ, illustrating reciprocal sound substitution.
rows.anchor: الجدث: القبر، وسمع فيه جدف بإبدال الثاء فاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Maskh» means transforming someone from one form into a hideous one.
rows.anchor: المسخ: تحويل من صورة إلى صورة منكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Ramīm» means decayed and crumbled.
rows.anchor: الرميم: البالي المفتت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that «We record their traces» was revealed about Banū Salima considering a move near the Prophet’s mosque is unsound; another exception proposed is the spending verse.
rows.anchor: حين أرادوا أن يتركوا ديارهم وينتقلوا إلى جوار مسجد الرسول، وليس زعما صحيحا

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: He says «Yā Sīn» is one of Muḥammad’s names, adducing the following declaration that he is among the messengers; al-Sayyid al-Ḥamawī cites poetry.
rows.anchor: قال ابن جبير هنا: إنه اسم من أسماء محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، ودليله إنك لمن المرسلين

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He explains the letters as «O human» in Ethiopic or the Tayy dialect, where «īsān» means person and its plural is «ayāsīn».
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: معناه يا إنسان بالحبشية، وعنه هو في لغة طيء

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group parses yāʾ as a vocative and sīn as a clipped remnant of «human».
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: يا حرف نداء، والسين مقامة مقام إنسان

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: If the Tayy explanation is authentic, he derives it from «yā anaysīn», clipped by frequent use, like shortening an oath formula.
rows.anchor: إن صح أن معناه يا إنسان في لغة طيء، فوجهه أن يكون أصله يا أنيسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The diminutive «unaysiyān» points to «insān», not «anaysīn»; the latter is unattested, the proposed vocative form is grammatically unsuitable, and a diminutive would be disrespectful of prophethood.
rows.anchor: ولا نعلمهم قالوا في تصغيره أنيسين، وعلى تقدير أنه بقية أنيسين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians disagree whether the abbreviated «m» in the oath expression comes from «ayman» or is itself an oath particle.
rows.anchor: ومن النحويين من يقول: إن م حرف قسم وليس مبقى من أيمن

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Readings vary in the vowelled yaʾ and in whether nūn is assimilated to the following wāw; other named readers pronounce it clearly or vowel the nūn.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: بفتح الياء وإمالتها محضا، وبين اللفظين. وقرأ الجمهور: بسكون النون

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says «Yā Sīn» is an oath; Abū Ḥātim infers fatḥa, while al-Zajjāj analyzes it as an imperative to recite the named sūra.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: يس قسم

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He reads the nūn with ḍamma and explains the expression as «O human» in Tayy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الكلبي: بضم النون، وقال هي بلغة طيء: يا إنسان

rows.speaker: السماك، وابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: They are also reported to read the nūn with kasra.
rows.anchor: وقرأ السماك، وابن أبي إسحاق أيضا: بكسرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If «Yā Sīn» is an oath, its case may be accusative, nominative as a subject, or genitive by an implied preposition according to Kūfan grammarians.
rows.anchor: وإذا قيل أنه قسم، فيجوز أن يكون معربا بالنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Ḥakīm» may be passive/intensive, an intensive form of «ruler», or mean possessing wisdom.
rows.anchor: والحكيم: إما فعيل بمعنى مفعل، كما تقول: عقدت العسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Upon a straight path» may be a second predicate, a circumstantial phrase for the Prophet or the messengers, or governed by «sent».
rows.anchor: على صراط: خبر ثان، أو في موضع الحال منه عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path is the law of Islam.
rows.anchor: والصراط المستقيم: شريعة الإسلام

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Readers differ on «tanzīl»: some use the accusative as a verbal noun, others the nominative as a predicate of an omitted subject, and others the genitive as a substitute for «Qurʾān» or a descriptive verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة، والأشهب، وعيسى: بخلاف عنهما وابن عامر، وحمزة، والكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «So you may warn» attaches to «revelation» or an implicit «We sent»; the object «what» may refer to the punishment warned of.
rows.anchor: لتنذر: متعلق بتنزيل أو بأرسلنا مضمرة. ما أنذر، قال عكرمة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He construes «what» as a relative pronoun, the punishment of which their ancestors were warned; Ibn ʿAṭiyya alternatively takes it as a verbal noun and the ancestors as early descendants of Ishmael.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: بمعنى الذي، أي الشيء الذي أنذره آباؤهم من العذاب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He reads «what» as a negation: their nearer ancestors received no warning and so remained heedless; warnings to remote ancestors remove the apparent contradiction.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ما نافية، أي أن آباءهم لم ينذروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fixed decree is commonly identified as God’s promise to fill Hell with jinn and humans; alternatives are a prior decree of punishment or the messengers’ established truth about monotheism.
rows.anchor: المشهور أن القول لأملأن جهنم من الجنة والناس أجمعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The chains are literal and describe the disbelievers’ afterlife state, not a metaphor; Abū Ḥayyān rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s objection that their sight will then be sharp.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: إنا جعلنا في أعناقهم أغلالا الآية هو حقيقة لا استعارة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس، وابن إسحاق
rows.claim: They treat the chains as a metaphor for God restraining the disbelievers who planned harm to the Messenger and preventing their plot.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وابن إسحاق: استعارة لحالة الكفرة الذين أرادوا الرسول بسوء

rows.speaker: الضحاك، والفراء
rows.claim: They interpret the shackled hand metaphorically as preventing people from spending in God’s cause.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك، والفراء: استعارة لمنعهم من النفقة في سبيل الله

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He says the verse came down when Abū Jahl tried to strike the Prophet with a large stone; the ensuing account describes his hands binding to his neck and his blindness.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: نزلت حين أراد أبو جهل ضربه بالحجر العظيم

rows.speaker: فرقة
rows.claim: Another group reads the chains as God preventing the disbelievers from believing; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers this because it fits the preceding statement that they will not believe.
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: استعارة لمنع الله إياهم من الإيمان وحوله بينهم وبينه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He makes the chains and barriers a metaphor for fixed disbelief: they neither turn their necks toward truth nor reflect on God’s signs.
rows.anchor: مثل تصميمهم على الكفر، وأنه لا سبيل إلى دعواهم بأن جعلهم كالمغلولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān detects a Muʿtazilī implication in al-Zamakhsharī’s account, which assigns the decisive acts to the disbelievers rather than God, unlike Sunni accounts of divine prevention.
rows.anchor: وفيه دسيسة الاعتزال. ألا ترى إلى قول أهل السنة استعارة لمنع الله إياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A «ghull» is what encircles the neck, connoting constraint, rebuke, torment, or captivity; hands may accompany the neck because they are bound with it.
rows.anchor: والغل ما أحاط بالعنق على معنى التعنيف والتضييق والتعذيب والأسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in «they are» apparently returns to the chains themselves, as the named subject.
rows.anchor: والظاهر عود الضمير في فهي إلى الأغلال

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He describes a broad collar reaching the chin and forcing the captive’s face upward; this posture is called «iqmāḥ».
rows.anchor: هي عريضة تبلغ بحرفها الأذقان، والذقن مجتمع اللحيين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains the posture mechanically: the collar’s joined ring and projecting bar under the chin prevent lowering the head, keeping the captive looking up.
rows.anchor: فلا تخليه يطاطىء رأسه ويوطىء قذاله، فلا يزال مقمحا

rows.speaker: الفراء، والزجاج
rows.claim: They explain «qamiḥ» as one who averts his gaze after raising his head.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: القمح الذي يغض بصره بعد رفع رأسه

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: He says a camel «qamaḥ» raises its head from a watering trough and does not drink; he cites a poem describing camels with raised heads.
rows.anchor: قمح قموحا: رفع رأسه عن الحوض ولم يشرب

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: He says a camel raises its head after drinking foul water; another explanation names the cold months «qimāḥ» because animals dislike the icy water, with two vowel variants.
rows.anchor: هو رفع البعير رأسه إذا شرب الماء الكريه ثم يعود

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He describes «qāmiḥ» as someone whose gaze is lifted toward the place of his feet.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: القامح: الطافح ببصره إلى موضع قدمه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He glosses the posture as raising the head and placing the hand over the mouth.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: الرافع الرأس، الواضح يده على فيه

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: He makes the pronoun refer to the hands, though not previously named: a neck-chain normally includes the hands and is called a «jāmiʿa» because it joins them.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: الضمير في فهي عائد على الأيدي، وإن لم يتقدم لها ذكر

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: He demonstrated the raised posture by placing his hands beneath his chin and raising his head.
rows.anchor: وأرى علي، كرم الله وجهه، الناس الأقماح، فجعل يديه تحت لحييه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He argues that the chains reaching the chins cause the raised posture; reading the pronoun as hands obscures that causation and abandons the apparent meaning.
rows.anchor: جعل الأقماح نتيجة قوله: فهي إلى الأذقان

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read «sud» with ḍamma on the sīn; a substantial set of readers use fatḥa in both places.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله، وعكرمة، والنخعي، وابن وثاب، وطلحة، وحمزة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «We covered them» with ghayn; another reported group reads with ʿayn, from blindness or weak sight, meaning that God placed a covering over their eyes.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: فأغشيناهم بالغين منقوطة وابن عباس، وعمر بن عبد العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warning benefits the one who follows the reminder—identified as the Qurʾān, or by Qatāda as admonition—and fears the Merciful in private, fearing loss of His blessings; such a person receives forgiveness and Paradise.
rows.anchor: إنما تنذر: أي إنذارا ينفع من اتبع الذكر، وهو القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After messengerhood, the passage names resurrection, another of the three foundations of faith; the third is divine unity.
rows.anchor: ولما ذكر تعالى الرسالة، وهي أحد الأصول الثلاثة التي بها يصير المكلف مؤمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «We give life to the dead» means raising them after death; al-Ḥasan and al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s interpretation as bringing people from shirk to faith is far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وأبعد الحسن والضحاك في قوله: إحياؤهم: إخراجهم من الشرك إلى الإيمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recording what people did is a metaphor for recompense and for the comprehensive knowledge fixed by writing; another recitation uses a passive verb.
rows.anchor: ونكتب ما قدموا، كناية عن المجازاة: أي ونحصي

rows.speaker: زر ومسروق
rows.claim: They read «and it is written» in the passive; «their traces» are their footsteps to the mosques.
rows.anchor: وقرأ زر ومسروق: ويكتب ما قدموا وآثارهم بالياء مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He explains the recorded traces as good and bad paths; another view distinguishes their prior bad deeds from the deeds left as traces.
rows.anchor: وقال: السير الحسنة والسيئة. وقيل: ما قدموا من السيئات وآثارهم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He includes lasting effects left after death: useful knowledge, books, endowments, buildings, or harmful policies, debased coinage, distractions, and any good or bad custom others follow.
rows.anchor: وما هلكوا عنه من أثر حسن، كعلم علموه، وكتاب صنفوه، أو حبيس أحبسوه

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «every thing» in the accusative by the resumptive construction; Abū al-Sammāl reads it nominative as a new subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: وكل شيء بالنصب على الاشتغال

rows.speaker: مجاهد، وقتادة، وابن زيد
rows.claim: They identify the «clear register» as the Preserved Tablet; another group understands it as records of deeds.
rows.anchor: والإمام المبين: اللوح المحفوظ، قاله مجاهد وقتادة وابن زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Strike a parable» was discussed at 2:26; the village is Antioch, and the source says there is no disagreement about the story’s setting.
rows.anchor: والقرية: أنطاكية، فلا خلاف في قصة أصحاب القرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Three messengers are collectively said to arrive even though their arrival times differed; the text then recounts sending two first.
rows.anchor: هم ثلاثة، جمعهم في المجيء، وإن اختلفوا في زمن المجيء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وكعب
rows.claim: They take the messengers as prophets sent by God; the recipients’ claim that they are ordinary humans supports this reading.
rows.anchor: وهذه المحاورة لا تكون إلا مع من أرسله الله، وهذا قول ابن عباس وكعب

rows.speaker: قتادة وغيرهم من الحواريين
rows.claim: They say Jesus sent the three disciples after the crucifixion episode, as his followers dispersed; the group reached idol-worshipping Antioch.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وغيرهم من الحواريين: بعثهم عيسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: وهب وكعب الأحبار
rows.claim: They identify the first two messengers as Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq; other names are reported by al-Naqqāsh and Muqātil.
rows.anchor: صادق وصدوق، قاله وهب وكعب الأحبار

rows.speaker: مجاهد وابن قتيبة
rows.claim: They explain «fa-ʿazzaznā» as strengthening and supporting the first two; related idioms describe firm camel flesh and rain compacting earth.
rows.anchor: فعززنا بثالث: أي قوينا وشددنا، قاله مجاهد وابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: الحسن، وأبو حيوة، وأبو بكر، والمفضل، وأبان
rows.claim: They read the verb with a light zāy; Abū ʿAlī explains this as «we prevailed», comparing the expression in 38:23.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وأبو حيوة، وأبو بكر، والمفضل، وأبان: بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the third messenger as Shamʿūn al-Ṣafā; Kaʿb and Wahb instead report Shalūm or Yūnus.
rows.anchor: والثالث شمعون الصفا، قاله ابن عباس. وقال كعب، ووهب: شلوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of «strengthened» is omitted: the third messenger strengthened the first two, and together they prevailed with argument and tactful invitation.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعول فعززنا مشددا، أي قويناهما بثالث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first claim «we are sent» begins an assertion without emphasis; the second adds emphatic lām as an answer to denial of revelation. The messengers entrust their truth to God and are responsible only for clear delivery.
rows.anchor: وجاء أولا مرسلون بغير لام لأنه ابتداء إخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clarity of the message is shown by signs in the story, including curing the congenitally blind and lepers and reviving the dead.
rows.anchor: من إبراء الأكمه والأبرص وإحياء الميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «We have taken you as an ill omen» means they regarded the messengers as a bad portent; the speaker reports explanations involving withheld rain or increased leprosy after denial.
rows.anchor: قالوا إنا تطيرنا بكم: أي تشاء منا

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He says rain was withheld from the people.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: احتبس عليهم المطر

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says the omen most likely reflects division and social discord, like Quraysh’s superstition about Muḥammad and the charge made against Moses.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن تطير هؤلاء كان سبب ما دخل فيهم من اختلاف الكلمة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains the superstition psychologically: people call what they desire blessed and what they dislike ill-omened, as in the Qurʾānic accounts of Pharaoh’s people and Meccan polytheists.
rows.anchor: وعادة الجهال أن يتمنوا بكل شيء مالوا إليه واشتهوه

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He paraphrases their accusation as saying that any misfortune they suffer is because of the messengers.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة: إن أصابنا شيء كان من أجلكم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: They threaten to stone the messengers; their promised painful punishment is burning.
rows.anchor: لنرجمنكم بالحجارة، قاله قتادة. عذاب أليم: هو الحريق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Your bird is with you» means your fate and what good or evil reaches you come from your own deeds and disbelief, not from the messengers.
rows.anchor: قالوا طائركم معكم: أي حظكم وما صار لكم من خير أو شر معكم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «ṭāʾirukum»; other readers use «ṭayrukum» or the assimilated source «iṭṭayyarukum».
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن، وابن هرمز، وعمرو بن عبيد، وزر بن حبيش: طيركم

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read two hamzas in «a-in dhukkirtum»; named readers variously lighten or ease the second, use one hamza, or insert a lengthened vowel, with a poetic witness.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: أإن ذكرتم بهمزتين، الأولى همزة الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first reading asks whether they take omens when warned; other hamza forms make the warning the cause of their superstition, while «wherever» readings leave or front the conditional answer.
rows.anchor: فالقراءة الأولى على معنى: إن ذكرتم تتطيرون

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «dhukkirtum» with a doubled kāf; a range of readers lighten it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: ذكرتم، بتشديد الكاف وأبو جعفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «You are an excessive people» means they exceed the bounds in error, which is why they meet misfortune.
rows.anchor: بل أنتم قوم مسرفون: مجاوزون الحد في ضلالكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وأبو مجلز وكعب الأحبار ومجاهد ومقاتل
rows.claim: They identify the man who came from the farthest part of town as Ḥabīb; reports differ about his lineage and whether he was a fuller, cobbler, or idol-carver.
rows.anchor: اسمه حبيب، قاله ابن عباس وأبو مجلز وكعب الأحبار ومجاهد ومقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accounts place him farming outside town, worshipping in a cave, or living with leprosy near a separate gate; after seventy years of fruitless idol worship, he accepts the messengers’ offer to pray and is cured.
rows.anchor: عبد الأصنام سبعين سنة يدعوهم لكشف ضره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After believing, he earned a living and divided it between his family and charity; when the townspeople moved to kill the messengers, he urged them to follow.
rows.anchor: فأقبل على التكسب، فإذا مشى، تصدق بكسبه، نصف لعياله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source says Ḥabīb later believed in Muḥammad despite a six-century interval, like Tubbaʿ and Waraqa; Ibn Abī Laylā names him among three early believers who never disbelieved.
rows.anchor: وحبيب هذا ممن آمن برسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، وبينهما ستمائة سنة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He cites Ibn Abī Laylā’s claim about the three early believers as a prophetic hadith; Abū Ḥayyān notes the report conflicts with the earlier account of Ḥabīb’s seventy years of idol worship.
rows.anchor: وأورد الزمخشري قول ابن أبي ليلى حديثا عن رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sūra mentions the man before the village, while al-Qaṣaṣ reverses that order as a rhetorical variation; «yasʿā» means walking on foot.
rows.anchor: وهنا تقدم: من أقصى المدينة، وفي القصص تأخر، وهو من التفنن في البلاغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The man most likely calls his people to follow only after he has believed; another account has him first ask whether the messengers demand payment, then persuade his people.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه لا يقول ذلك إلا بعد تقدم إيمانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He urges following those who ask no worldly wage and are guided by God, promising both preservation of worldly interests and guidance toward good in this life and the next.
rows.anchor: وهم على هدى من الله. أمرهم باتباع المرسلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some grammarians treat «who» as a substitute for «the messengers»; most reserve substitution for a prepositional phrase and analyze such cases as syntactic following.
rows.anchor: وقد أجاز بعض النحويين في من أن تكون بدلا من المرسلين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse implies that taking payment for an obligatory religious act, such as prayer, is blameworthy.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: اتبعوا من لا يسئلكم أجرا، دليل على نقص من يأخذ أجرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥabīb couches the appeal as advice to himself to soften the people and show sincere concern; «why should I not worship my Creator?» means «why do you not?», as the shift to «you return» confirms.
rows.anchor: فأبرزه في صورة نصحه لنفسه، وهو يريد نصحهم ليتلطف بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idols cannot benefit or harm: they lack standing for effective intercession and the power to rescue, two distinct grounds for rejecting them.
rows.anchor: فإن أرادكم الله بضر، وشفعت لكم، لم تنفع شفاعتهم، ولم يقدروا على إنقاذكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers differ on the first-person yāʾ in «if the Merciful wills harm for me»; the opened yāʾ is an annexed pronoun deleted in speech to avoid two unvowelled letters, not a causative prefix as al-Zamakhsharī supposes.
rows.anchor: والذي في كتب القراء الشواذ أنها ياء الإضافة المحذوفة خطا ونطقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If he abandoned the Creator and adopted idols, he would plainly be in error before any sound-minded observer.
rows.anchor: إني إذا، إن لم أعبد الذي فطرني واتخذت آلهة من دونه، في حيرة واضحة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وكعب ووهب
rows.claim: The man directly addresses his people: he believes in the Lord they denied, asks them to hear and obey, and reminds them worship belongs to their Creator.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الخطاب بالكاف والميم وبالواو، وهو لقومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view makes «hear me» address the messengers as witnesses; another makes both «your Lord» and «hear me» address the messengers as he flees his pursuers and asks them to attest his faith.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خاطب بقوله فاسمعون الرسل، على جهة الاستشهاد بهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «Enter the Garden» apparently is a real command; alternatively it reports that he deserves it, which would mean entrance after Resurrection, and the text never explicitly says he was killed.
rows.anchor: وقيل: معناه وجبت لك الجنة، فهو خبر بأنه قد استحق دخولها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says God raised the man to heaven when his people tried to kill him; he remains alive in Paradise until its end, then enters it again after resurrection.
rows.anchor: فقال الحسن: لما أراد قومه قتله، رفعه الله إلى السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says his captors kept him talking before a ruler, then trampled him to death and threw him into a well called al-Rass.
rows.anchor: فوثبوا عليه فقتلوه بوطء الأرجل حتى خرج قلبه من دبره

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He says the people stoned the man while he prayed, «God, guide my people».
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: رموه بالحجارة وهو يقول:

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He says the people threw him into a pit and covered him with earth until he died.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: رموه في حفرة، وردوا التراب عليه فمات

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He says they burned and hung him at the city gate; other accounts say he was sawn apart.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن: حرقوه حرقا، وعلقوه في باب المدينة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says God brought the man into Paradise alive, deriving it from the promise that the martyrs live and are provided for.
rows.anchor: وعن قتادة: أدخله الله الجنة، وهو فيها حي يرزق

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s copy says most read «hear me» with fatḥa on nūn, which Abū Ḥātim calls impossible for an imperative; Abū Ḥayyān suspects a copying error, since readers use kasra.
rows.anchor: القراء مجمعون فيما أعلم على كسر النون، سبعتهم وشواذهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says omitted, widely transmitted reports establish that the people killed the man, after which Paradise was shown to him and he wished his people knew of his vindication.
rows.anchor: هنا محذوف تواترت به الأحاديث والروايات، وهو أنهم قتلوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive «it was said, enter Paradise» answers an implied question about his fate; the man wishes his people knew so they might believe, or so they would regret having opposed him.
rows.anchor: قيل ادخل الجنة كأنه جواب لسائل عن حاله عند لقاء ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People naturally want hometown peers to see their good fortune; he illustrates this with a vizier returning to his small Egyptian village and cites a poem about glory being most loved when won at home.
rows.anchor: وموجود في طباع النشر أن من أصاب خيرا في غير موطنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The «mā» in «by what my Lord forgave me» is a verbal noun, expressing his wish that his people know of forgiveness and honor; making it a relative pronoun wrongly makes him wish they knew the sins.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ما في قوله: بما غفر لي ربي مصدرية

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: He permits «mā» as an interrogative, meaning «by what did my Lord forgive me?»; al-Kisāʾī objects that the expected form drops the alif.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الفراء أن تكون ما استفهاما. وقال الكسائي: لو صح هذا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He allows the question to refer to the man’s endurance with his people in defense of religion; Abū Ḥayyān says retaining alif in an interrogative after a preposition is normally poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: والمشهور أن إثبات الألف في ما الاستفهامية، إذا دخل عليها حرف جر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «al-mukramīn» with a still kāf and light rāʾ; another reading doubles the rāʾ and opens the kāf.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: من المكرمين، مشدد الراء مفتوح الكاف والجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God destroyed the people of Ḥabīb with one cry from Gabriel, warning Quraysh of the same fate; no heavenly army such as stones or wind was needed.
rows.anchor: أخبر تعالى بإهلاك قوم حبيب بصيحة واحدة صاح بهم جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «After him» marks the starting point: God sent no further messenger or reprimand after they killed him, but destroyed them immediately.
rows.anchor: أي لم يرسل إليهم رسولا، ولا عاتبهم بعد قتله، بل عاجلهم بالهلاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: «What We were sending down» is negative, restating that no heavenly army was required; God gives different peoples different forms of punishment.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن ما في قوله: وما كنا منزلين نافية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He construes «mā» as a relative coordinated with «army», meaning no army and none of what God sent to comparable peoples; Abū Ḥayyān rejects the grammar because a definite relative cannot coordinate with the indefinite after an extra «min».
rows.anchor: وقالت فرقة: ما اسم معطوف على جند. قال ابن عطية: أي من جند

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: He proposes that «mā» is redundant, making the phrase mean «and We were indeed sending down»; Abū Ḥayyān dismisses this analysis.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: ويجوز أن تكون ما زائدة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most read «it was only a cry» with accusative «cry», taking «kānat» as incomplete with an omitted subject such as seizure or punishment.
rows.anchor: وقرأ: إن كانت إلا صيحة، بنصب الصيحة، وكان ناقصة

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر، وشيبة، ومعاذ بن الحارث القارئ
rows.claim: They read «cry» nominative in both places and take «kānat» as a complete verb meaning it happened; grammarians differ on feminine agreement when the subject follows «except».
rows.anchor: على أن كانت تامة، أي ما خدثت أو وقعت إلا صيحة

rows.speaker: الحسن، ومالك بن دينار، وأبو رجاء، والجحدري، وقتادة، وأبو حيوة، وابن أبي عبلة، وأبو بحرية
rows.claim: They read «you see only their dwellings» with feminine verb agreement; the common reading uses masculine agreement, a parallel point of grammatical variation.
rows.anchor: لا ترى إلا مساكنهم بالتاء، والقراءة المشهورة بالياء
